**Welcome to the Transcriptomics week of 27200 Data-driven Bioengineering!**

This session is **Week 6** of the course (lecture: **Thursday, 08 October 2026**), part of the omics block. The theme of the week: **transcript abundance as a dynamic - but incomplete - regulatory readout**.

We cover the theory behind RNA sequencing and the full practical workflow - from raw reads to biological interpretation: the RNA-seq workflow and count matrices, normalization, batch effects revisited, PCA, differential expression, and what transcriptomics reflects and misses.

The material is designed for people with **no or little practical experience** in transcriptomic analysis using RNA sequencing (RNA-seq).

**Objectives**

* Theory on Illumina short-read sequencing technology for transcriptome analysis
* Theory and practical sessions for
   * RNA-seq data processing using the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline
   * Quality control and exploratory analysis (normalization, PCA, sample correlation)
   * Differential expression analysis with DESeq2 - design formulas, shrinkage, multiple testing
   * Enrichment analysis (GSEA, plus ORA in the advanced bacterial track) - gaining biological insights from transcriptomic data
   * Critically assessing what transcript abundance can and cannot tell you about biology

**Datasets**

* 🧑‍🔬 *Homo sapiens* - airway smooth muscle cells treated with dexamethasone (paired donor design). This is the one we work on together.
* 🦠 *Staphylococcus aureus* - biofilm vs planktonic over time, strains USA-100 and USA-500. Advanced material, if you want to go further.

:::boxy
**Work through the human dataset**: the three notebooks in order (**01 quality control → 02 differential expression → 03 functional enrichment**). Each one saves results that the next one reads, so the order matters. Depth beats coverage: it is better to interpret one dataset well than to rush. If you finish early, the *S. aureus* material takes the same ideas further, with a time course and two strains.
:::

:::boxy
You can also explore the [27200 Data Driven Bioengineering - Transcriptomics repository](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering)
:::

**Draft agenda** (4-hour block: lecture + guided exercises, in groups of 4)

| Time | Session |
|---|---|
| ☕ **8:00–8:15** | Welcome and setup. **Start the pipeline run now** - it takes about 25 minutes and finishes while we talk |
| 🔬 **8:15–10:00** | Lectures: sequencing and the RNA-seq workflow; count matrices, normalization, PCA and differential expression (with a short break) |
| 💻 **10:00–11:50** | Exercises: quality control, then differential expression and functional enrichment |
| 🏁 **11:50–12:00** | Wrap-up: key insight + muddy point |


:::boxy

docker run --rm -it -p 8888:8888 -v "$PWD":/work -w /work \

### Option 3: your own R installation

Only sensible if you are comfortable with R and with sorting out package installations
yourself, Bioconductor ones included. If it breaks on the morning of the class, switch to
a Codespace rather than lose the session to it. Install the packages well in advance:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# DSP Transcriptomics Workshop – Package Installation Script
# ============================================================
# Run this script ONCE before the workshop to install all
# required R packages. Works on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
# Tested with R >= 4.3.
# ============================================================

## ---- 0. Helper: install only if missing --------------------

install_if_missing <- function(pkg, installer, ...) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    message("Installing: ", pkg)
    installer(pkg, ...)
  } else {
    message("Already installed: ", pkg)
  }
}

## ---- 1. CRAN packages --------------------------------------

cran_pkgs <- c(
  "tidyverse",
  "reshape2",
  "RColorBrewer",
  "pheatmap",
  "knitr",
  "kableExtra",
  "DT",
  "ggpubr",
  "gggenes",     # operon plots (S. aureus)
  "msigdbr",     # MSigDB gene sets for GSEA (human)
  "ragg",        # draws plots with proper unicode
  "remotes"      # needed for GitHub installs below
)

for (pkg in cran_pkgs) {
  install_if_missing(pkg, install.packages,
                     dependencies = TRUE)
}

## ---- 2. Bioconductor packages ------------------------------

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("BiocManager")
}
# Pin to the release that matches R 4.4; BiocManager picks the right
# version automatically, but you can force with: BiocManager::install(version = "3.19")

bioc_pkgs <- c(
  "DESeq2",
  "apeglm",       # recommended shrinkage estimator used with DESeq2
  "fgsea",
  "EnhancedVolcano"
)

for (pkg in bioc_pkgs) {
  install_if_missing(pkg, BiocManager::install,
                     update = FALSE, ask = FALSE)
}

## ---- 3. GitHub packages ------------------------------------

# mulea is not on CRAN/Bioconductor yet
if (!requireNamespace("mulea", quietly = TRUE)) {
  message("Installing mulea from GitHub (ELTEbioinformatics/mulea)")
  remotes::install_github("ELTEbioinformatics/mulea")
} else {
  message("Already installed: mulea")
}

## ---- 4. Verification ---------------------------------------

all_pkgs <- c(
  cran_pkgs,
  bioc_pkgs,
  "mulea"
)
# remove helper-only packages from the check list
check_pkgs <- setdiff(all_pkgs, "remotes")

cat("\n========== Installation check ==========\n")
ok  <- character(0)
nok <- character(0)

for (pkg in check_pkgs) {
  if (requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    ok <- c(ok, pkg)
  } else {
    nok <- c(nok, pkg)
  }
}

cat("OK  (", length(ok),  "):", paste(ok,  collapse = ", "), "\n\n")

if (length(nok) > 0) {
  cat("FAILED (", length(nok), "):", paste(nok, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("Please re-run the script or install the above packages manually.\n")
} else {
  cat("All packages installed successfully. You are ready for the workshop!\n")
}
cat("=========================================\n")
```

# Instructions

:::boxy
[nf-core rnaseq pipeline](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.27.0/docs/usage/)
:::

**Topics covered**

-   RNA-seq data processing with the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline
-   Mapping of short reads (Bowtie2 for bacteria, STAR for human) and quantification with Salmon
-   Quality control and exploratory data analysis
-   Differential expression analysis (DESeq2)
-   Functional enrichment analysis (GSEA for human; ORA as well in the advanced bacterial track)

**Data**

All datasets are bulk RNA-seq. The codes are in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering).

-   🦠 ***Staphylococcus aureus*** - biofilm vs planktonic lifestyle over time, strains USA-100 and USA-500, from [Tomlinson *et al.*, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1099/mgen.0.000598) (GEO: [GSE163153](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE163153), PRJNA685119).
    Reference genomes are strain-specific: **USA-100** → N315 ([GCF_000009645.1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000009645.1/)); **USA-500** → USA300_FPR3757 ([GCF_000013465.1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/GCF_000013465.1/)), its closest finished relative, as in the paper.
-   🧑‍🔬 ***Homo sapiens*** - primary airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells treated with dexamethasone, paired donor design, from [Himes *et al.*, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0099625) (GEO: [GSE52778](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE52778), PRJNA229998).
    Reference genome: GRCh38 primary assembly, [GENCODE](https://www.gencodegenes.org/human/) v50 annotation.

Both count matrices were produced with the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline and are provided **precomputed** in the repository, so the analysis notebooks start from those. For the hands-on pipeline run below we use two sub-sampled human samples, so it finishes within class time.

AI-assisted workflows are allowed - and encouraged - in this course, as long as you **validate what the AI tells you**.

It can read the files in this repository, explain code, and help you debug errors.

**Things to try**

- Ask: *"Explain what the design formula `~ donor + condition` does in the human differential expression notebook, and why donor is included."* Then check the explanation against the chapter text.
- Ask: *"Why does the quality control script round the Salmon counts before DESeq2 instead of truncating them?"* Verify the answer in the code.
- When a notebook cell errors, paste the error and ask the agent to diagnose it - then make sure you understand the fix before applying it.
- Ask an agent to interpret one of your PCA plots, and decide which parts of its answer the data actually supports.

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Ground rules:</strong> AI assistants confidently make mistakes - treat every answer as a hypothesis to verify, not a fact. Never paste passwords, tokens, or API keys into a prompt. And you must be able to explain any AI-assisted result yourself.
</div>



## Data processing using the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline

**Sources of data and genome files**

For the hands-on run we use two human samples, one dexamethasone-treated and one untreated from the same donor, sub-sampled to 50,000 reads each, against a 5 Mb slice of chromosome 19. Both keep the run inside class time. Nothing has to be downloaded: the reads and the genome files are already in the repository.

-   Reads: [PRJNA229998 / GSE52778](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE52778), sub-sampled, under `data/seq_files_subsampled/PRJNA229998_GSE52778_human/`
-   Genome sequence and annotation: GRCh38 chr19:48,115,444-53,115,443 with the matching [GENCODE](https://www.gencodegenes.org/human/) v50 annotation, under `data/genome_files/human/`

The count matrices analysed in the following chapters were made with this same pipeline on the **full** datasets: all time points for both *S. aureus* strains with the prokaryotic profile, and the human samples with STAR (human genes have introns, so a splice-aware aligner is needed). Those outputs, along with their MultiQC reports, are provided under `data/`, so the analysis notebooks can start directly from the counts.

<!--chapter:end:02_introduction.Rmd-->

# Running the nf-core/rnaseq pipeline v3.27.0

**This is the first thing you do today** - start it during the welcome, before the
lectures, and it will be finished by the time the exercises begin. Before analysing
anyone else's count matrix, you produce one yourself, so that the table the notebooks
start from is not a black box.

Processing a whole dataset needs more compute than we have in a classroom, so you run
two human airway smooth muscle samples from the dexamethasone experiment, one treated
and one untreated, sub-sampled to 50,000 reads each. The reference is a 5 Mb slice of
chromosome 19 rather than the whole genome, for the same reason.

<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ What this run is, and what it is not.</strong> Two files of 50,000 reads
  against 5 Mb of one chromosome are enough to watch the pipeline work and to read its
  quality report. They are far too few to draw biology from, so <strong>you will not
  analyse your own output</strong>. Once you have seen how reads become counts, the
  notebooks pick up from the full count matrices, made with this same pipeline, which are
  already in <code>data/</code>. If you go looking for your pipeline output in notebook
  01, you will not find it - that is expected.
</div>

We use pipeline release [v3.27.0](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.27.0) with the
`star_salmon` aligner: STAR for alignment and Salmon for quantification. Human
genes have introns, so the aligner has to be splice-aware. (For bacteria this is
unnecessary, which is why the advanced *S. aureus* track uses the `prokaryotic`
profile and Bowtie2 instead.)

**To process the data, run the following command:**

```bash
bash 00_pipeline/00_nfcore_rnaseq_processing_human.sh
```

That script runs the command below. Paths are shortened here for readability; in the
script they are written out in full from `/workspaces/`, which is where the repository
sits inside a Codespace.

```bash
nextflow run 'https://github.com/nf-core/rnaseq' \
    -r 3.27.0 \
    -profile docker \
    --aligner star_salmon \
    --input  'data/seq_files_subsampled/PRJNA229998_GSE52778_human/samplesheet_PRJNA229998_subsampled_2samples.csv' \
    --outdir 'results/human/nfcore_rnaseq_processing_downsampled' \
    --fasta  'data/genome_files/human/chr19_GRCh38_48115444-53115443.fna.gz' \
    --gtf    'data/genome_files/human/chr19_GRCh38_48115444-53115443.gtf.gz' \
    --gtf_group_features 'gene_id' \
    --featurecounts_feature_type 'exon' \
    -c 00_pipeline/custom.config \
    -c 00_pipeline/human_demo.config
```

**What the arguments mean:**

-   `-r`: which release of the pipeline to use
-   `-profile`: run the tools in `docker` containers
-   `--aligner`: `star_salmon`, i.e. STAR for alignment and Salmon for quantification
-   `--input`: the sample sheet, listing each sample and its two fastq files
-   `--outdir`: where results go (the folder is created for you)
-   `--fasta`: the genome sequence, here the chromosome 19 slice
-   `--gtf`: the matching annotation
-   `-c`: two small config files. One caps CPUs and memory so the run fits in a
    Codespace; the other sets a handful of switches that cannot be passed on the
    command line.

It takes about **20 to 25 minutes**.

<div class="warning">
  <strong>⚠️ Free the disk space afterwards.</strong> A Codespace does not have room for
  two pipeline runs. This one fills roughly half the disk, almost all of it intermediate
  files that you do not need once the run has finished. When it completes, run:

```bash
rm -rf work .nextflow*
```

  This keeps everything in <code>results/</code> and throws away the rest. The script does it
  for you when the run succeeds, and also removes the Docker images the pipeline pulled, which
  are nearly 22 GB of the 32 GB disk. Two things you give up: <code>-resume</code>, because
  Nextflow re-uses <code>work</code> to skip finished steps, and the containers, so running the
  other dataset afterwards re-downloads them. Both are fair trades here, because the run is
  short and otherwise the disk ends the morning full.
</div>

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> If you finish early and want to see how a bacterial dataset
  differs, run the cleanup above first, then
  <code>bash 00_pipeline/00_nfcore_rnaseq_processing_saureus.sh</code>. It uses two
  <em>S. aureus</em> USA-100 samples and the <code>prokaryotic</code> profile, and takes
  about 10 minutes. Without the cleanup it will run out of disk part-way through.
</div>

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> You can also set parameters through the nf-core website instead of typing them.
  Go to the [pipeline page](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/3.27.0), press **Launch version 3.27.0**, fill in the form,
  and it generates a config file you can pass to Nextflow.
</div>

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> The counts the notebooks use were made with this same pipeline on the full
  datasets: the human samples against the whole GRCh38 genome, and all three time points for both
  <em>S. aureus</em> strains with Bowtie2. The scripts for those runs are in
  <code>00_pipeline/</code> if you want to see the exact commands.
</div>

## Structure of the output directory

Results are written to `results/human/nfcore_rnaseq_processing_downsampled`.
The top level looks like this:

```
.
├── fastqc
├── fq_lint
├── multiqc
├── pipeline_info
├── star_salmon
└── trimgalore
```

What each folder holds:

-   **`star_salmon`** - the important one. Alignments (`.bam`), per-sample Salmon quantification, and the merged count matrices for the whole run. `salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv` and `salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds` are what an analysis like the next chapter starts from.
-   **`fastqc`** - read quality reports, before (`raw`) and after (`trim`) trimming.
-   **`fq_lint`** - format checks on the fastq files.
-   **`multiqc`** - everything above gathered into one report. Start here.
-   **`pipeline_info`** - what ran, for how long, with which software versions. This is your reproducibility record.
-   **`trimgalore`** - adapter and quality trimming reports.

A closer look inside `star_salmon`, for one sample:

```
star_salmon
├── N052611_dexamethasone/              # per-sample Salmon output
│   ├── quant.sf                        #   transcript-level estimates
│   └── quant.genes.sf                  #   gene-level estimates
├── N052611_dexamethasone.sorted.bam
├── N052611_dexamethasone.sorted.bam.bai
├── log/                                # STAR alignment logs
├── samtools_stats/                     # alignment summaries per sample
├── deseq2_qc/                          # a quick PCA and sample distances
├── salmon.merged.gene_counts.tsv       # merged counts, genes x samples
├── salmon.merged.gene_tpm.tsv          # merged TPM
├── salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds
└── salmon.merged.tx2gene.tsv           # transcript to gene mapping
```

## Reading the MultiQC report

MultiQC collects the quality metrics from every step into a single page, so you
can compare all samples side by side instead of opening reports one at a time.

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 About half your reads map, not the 80 to 90 per cent a full run gives.</strong>
  The reference is 5 Mb of one chromosome, and the reads were chosen from that region so
  that the demo produces a usable count matrix. Mates whose partner falls outside the
  window, and reads crossing the window's edges, still have nowhere to go. A mapping rate
  only means something once you know what was mapped against what.
</div>

A two-sample run is still too small to judge an experiment by, so we will also look at a
report from a full dataset, processed before the course. Every dataset in `data/` has one:

| Dataset | MultiQC report |
|---|---|
| Human ASM, 8 samples | [data-02-Homo_sapiens_multiqc_report.html](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-02-Homo_sapiens/hasapiens/multiqc/data-02-Homo_sapiens_multiqc_report.html) |
| *S. aureus* USA-100, 32 samples | [data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus_USA100_multiqc_report.html](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus/USA-100/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus_USA100_multiqc_report.html) |
| *S. aureus* USA-500, 32 samples | [data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus_USA500_multiqc_report.html](https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus/USA-500/data-01-Staphylococcus_aureus_USA500_multiqc_report.html) |

Use the human one today; the two bacterial reports belong to the advanced track.

A MultiQC report is an HTML page and VS Code cannot display one inside a Codespace. In the
Codespace, right-click the file in the explorer and choose **Download**, then open the
downloaded file in your browser. Straight from GitHub, click **Download raw file** instead.

Things worth looking at:

- The general statistics table at the top, one row per sample
- FastQC metrics: read quality, GC content, adapter content, duplication, before and after trimming
- How many reads aligned, per sample
- The PCA and sample-distance heatmap from DESeq2
- Software versions, at the very end

Spend a few minutes going through it. Use the menu on the left to move around.
We will talk about what you found afterwards.

:::boxy
Sample names tell you the donor and the treatment, for example
`N052611_dexamethasone` is donor N052611 treated with dexamethasone, and
`N052611_untreated` is the matching untreated sample from the same donor.
:::

# Quality Control

This report covers the quality control and exploratory analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from primary human airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells treated with dexamethasone, from [Himes *et al.*, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0099625) (GEO: GSE52778, PRJNA229998).

The list of contrasts of interest is:

:::boxy
- Dexamethasone (treatment) vs untreated (control)
:::

**Topics covered**

-   Exploratory data analyses
-   Sanity Checks

**Data**

-   Reference genome: human GRCh38 primary assembly with the GENCODE v50 annotation.

-   Input data is the output from the [nf-core/rnaseq pipeline](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/) `salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds` (STAR + Salmon).

<div class="note">
<strong>📘 Note:</strong> Key points about this dataset:
<ul>
<li>Reads are aligned with a splice-aware aligner (STAR), appropriate for spliced human transcripts</li>
<li>The reference GTF carries gene symbols, so genes are labelled directly (no ID conversion needed)</li>
<li>Enrichment analysis (a later script) uses GSEA with the MSigDB Reactome gene sets</li>
<li>Cells come from four donors → donor is a candidate confounder in the design (addressed below)</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="note">
<strong>📘 Note on this experiment:</strong> The full dataset contains four treatment arms per donor
(untreated, albuterol, dexamethasone, albuterol+dexamethasone). Following the study's primary
comparison, this workshop uses only <strong>dexamethasone vs untreated</strong> (n = 4 per group).
Because each donor contributes one treated and one untreated sample, the design is <strong>paired</strong>.
</div>

**Explanation of the QC analysis 🧾**

This document guides you through the standard QC pipeline for bulk RNA-seq data processed with [nf-core/rnaseq](https://nf-co.re/rnaseq/) `STAR` + `Salmon`. It is structured to be both educational and reproducible.


## Setup the Environment

::: {style="background:#d1ecf1;border-left:4px solid #0c5460;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;"}
<strong>📌 Remember:</strong> Load all libraries at the start of every session before running any analysis.
:::

```{r human-qc-libraries-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(reshape2)
library(DESeq2)
library(ggpubr)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(pheatmap)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(DT)
```

### Getting the Metadata

The metadata file describes the experimental design: which sample belongs to which donor and treatment group. This information is essential for `DESeq2` to model expression differences correctly.

```{r human-qc-load-metadata-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

git_root <- system("git rev-parse --show-toplevel", intern = TRUE)

samples_info <- read.table(
  file.path(git_root, "data", "data-02-Homo_sapiens", "metadata", "metadata.tsv"),
  header      = TRUE,
  sep         = "\t",
  check.names = TRUE
)
```

::: {style="background:#fff3cd;border-left:4px solid #ffc107;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;"}
<strong>💡 Tip:</strong> Use the interactive table below to verify your sample metadata before proceeding.
:::

```{r human-qc-view-metadata-0, echo=TRUE, include=TRUE, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

DT::datatable(
  data       = samples_info,
  rownames   = FALSE,
  extensions = c('Buttons', 'Scroller'),
  options    = list(
    dom         = 'Bfrtip',
    buttons     = c('copy', 'csv'),
    deferRender = TRUE,
    scrollX     = TRUE,
    scrollY     = 200,
    scroller    = TRUE
  ),
  caption = 'Sample metadata - Human ASM (dexamethasone vs untreated)'
)
```



<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Before you start: look at the pipeline's own QC.</strong> Everything below starts from a
  count matrix, which hides how the reads behaved. The nf-core run that produced it wrote a MultiQC
  report covering read quality, trimming, alignment rates and duplication for all eight samples:
  <a href="https://github.com/biosustain/dsp_transcriptomics_27200-Data-driven-bioengineering/blob/main/data/data-02-Homo_sapiens/hasapiens/multiqc/data-02-Homo_sapiens_multiqc_report.html">data-02-Homo_sapiens_multiqc_report.html</a>,
  under <code>data/data-02-Homo_sapiens/hasapiens/multiqc/</code>. It is an HTML page, which VS Code
  cannot display inside a Codespace: right-click the file in the explorer, choose
  <strong>Download</strong>, and open it in your own browser. If something is wrong at that level, no
  amount of careful modelling afterwards will rescue it.
</div>

### Loading Count Data

The nf-core/rnaseq pipeline was run with `STAR` for alignment and `Salmon` for quantification. We load the `SummarizedExperiment` object produced by the pipeline, extract the raw count matrix, and assign gene symbols as row names.

<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ Important:</strong> Salmon returns estimated counts, which are not integers. DESeq2 requires integer counts, so we round (not truncate) before building the object. This matches the tximport convention used by nf-core/differentialabundance.
</div>


::: {style="background:#fff3cd;border-left:4px solid #ffc107;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;"}
<strong>💡 Tip:</strong> If you are unsure which assay name or rowData columns are available in your RDS, inspect them first with <code>assayNames(count_x)</code> and <code>names(rowData(count_x))</code>.
:::

```{r human-qc-load-counts-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

count_x <- readRDS(
  file.path(git_root, "data", "data-02-Homo_sapiens", "hasapiens", "star_salmon",
            "salmon.merged.gene.SummarizedExperiment.rds")
)

# Inspect what is available (uncomment to explore):
# assayNames(count_x); names(rowData(count_x))

count_genes <- assay(count_x, assayNames(count_x)[1])

gene_symbols <- rowData(count_x)$gene_name
gene_ids     <- rowData(count_x)$gene_id

gene_symbols_saved <- ifelse(
  !is.na(gene_symbols) & nchar(gene_symbols) > 0,
  make.unique(as.character(gene_symbols)),
  make.unique(as.character(gene_ids))
)

# Salmon estimates are fractional -> round to nearest integer for DESeq2
count_genes <- as.matrix(count_genes)
mode(count_genes) <- "numeric"        # ensure numeric, not character
count_genes <- round(count_genes)
storage.mode(count_genes) <- "integer"
rownames(count_genes) <- gene_symbols_saved

cat("Dimensions (genes × samples):", dim(count_genes), "\n")
print(head(rownames(count_genes)))
print(colnames(count_genes))

# Report what the gene_id / gene_name columns actually contain.
# This pipeline used the GENCODE GTF, so gene_id holds ENSEMBL IDs and
# gene_name holds symbols. Confirm here:
cat("\nExample gene_id  :", paste(head(gene_ids, 3), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Example gene_name:", paste(head(gene_symbols, 3), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("gene_id look like ENSEMBL? :",
    any(grepl("^ENSG", head(gene_ids, 50))), "\n")
```

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> This dataset was processed against the <strong>GENCODE</strong> v50 GTF (GRCh38), so
  <code>gene_id</code> holds ENSEMBL IDs and <code>gene_name</code> holds gene <strong>symbols</strong>
  (e.g. <code>TSPAN6</code>). We use the symbols as row names. Symbols are exactly what
  MSigDB accepts, so no ID conversion is needed downstream. The check above prints the
  actual values so you can confirm this on your own RDS.
</div>

```{r human-qc-save-idmap-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Persist gene_id <-> gene_name map for downstream scripts
id_map <- data.frame(
  gene_id     = as.character(gene_ids),
  gene_symbol = gene_symbols_saved,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
dir.create(file.path(git_root, "results", "human"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(id_map, file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "gene_id_symbol_map.rds"))
```

## Preparing the Data

Before building the `DESeq2` object we:

1.  Subset the count matrix to the samples in the metadata (dexamethasone + untreated only - the albuterol arms are excluded).
2.  Set factor levels so that `control` is the **reference level** (the denominator in fold-change calculations).
3.  Set `donor` as a factor (needed for the paired design).
4.  Align the sample order between the count matrix and the metadata - `DESeq2` requires these to match exactly.

```{r human-qc-prepare-data-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
condition_levels   <- c("control", "treatment")
samples_info$group <- factor(samples_info$group, levels = condition_levels)
samples_info$donor <- factor(samples_info$donor)

# Subset count matrix to the 8 samples of interest (drop albuterol arms)
keep_samples <- intersect(samples_info$sample, colnames(count_genes))
missing      <- setdiff(samples_info$sample, colnames(count_genes))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop("⛔ Metadata samples not found in count matrix: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
}
count_genes <- count_genes[, keep_samples, drop = FALSE]

# Order metadata to match the count matrix columns exactly
samples_info <- samples_info[match(colnames(count_genes), samples_info$sample), ]

print(data.frame(count_col    = colnames(count_genes),
                 metadata_row = samples_info$sample,
                 donor        = samples_info$donor,
                 group        = samples_info$group))
```


### Creating the DESeqDataSet

The `DESeqDataSet` (DDS) holds the raw count matrix, sample metadata, and the design formula.

::: note
<strong>📘 Note:</strong> **Design choice.** Because each donor provides both a treated and an untreated
sample, donor is a paired/blocking factor. The recommended design is `~ donor + condition`, which
removes between-donor baseline differences before testing the treatment effect. The object saved here
carries that design; script 02 derives a simple `~ condition` version from it so the two can be compared
for teaching.
:::

```{r human-qc-make-dds-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
samples_info$condition <- factor(samples_info$group,
                                 levels = c("control", "treatment"))

# Primary (recommended) design: paired on donor
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = count_genes,
  colData   = samples_info,
  design    = ~ donor + condition
)
```


<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> The design formula uses R's formula syntax, where the tilde (`~`, pronounced **"TIL-duh"**)
means **"is modelled by"**. So `~ donor + condition` reads as: *"gene expression is modelled by
donor and condition"*.

In a general linear model, the tilde separates the **response variable** (left side) from
the **predictors** (right side). For example:

- `gene_expression ~ condition` - model expression as a function of condition only
- `gene_expression ~ donor + condition` - adjust for donor, then test condition

In DESeq2, the left side is omitted because the count matrix is already the response - you only need to specify which variables explain the differences between samples.
The variable of interest (`condition`) goes **last**; the terms before it are adjusted for.
</div>

## Sanity Checks

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> Always do a sanity check!
</div>


**Library sizes**

Before anything else, check how many reads ended up in each sample. DESeq2 needs
**raw, un-normalised integer counts**; if you feed it TPM or FPKM the results are wrong.

```{r human-qc-check-raw-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
options(scipen = 999)

barplot(colSums(count_genes),
        main   = "Library sizes (total counts per sample)",
        ylab   = "Total raw counts",
        xlab   = NULL,
        col    = "steelblue",
        las    = 2,
        names.arg = colnames(count_genes))
```

:::boxy
Samples differ in depth, which is exactly what the size factors further down correct for.
What would worry you is one sample far below the rest: too few reads means too little
information about that sample, whatever you do afterwards.
:::

### Pre-filtering Low-count Genes

Genes with very few counts across all samples carry no statistical power and inflate the multiple testing burden. We remove genes that do not have at least 10 counts in a minimum number of samples (equal to the size of the smallest group).

The human genome has roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes plus many non-coding ones, and a large fraction are not expressed in ASM cells - expect a substantial number to be filtered out.

```{r human-qc-prefilter-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

smallestGroupSize <- min(table(samples_info$condition))

cat("Smallest group size   :", smallestGroupSize, "\n")
cat("Filtering threshold   : at least 10 counts in", smallestGroupSize, "or more samples\n")

keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize
n_before <- nrow(dds)
dds  <- dds[keep, ]

cat("Genes before filtering:", n_before, "\n")
cat("Genes after  filtering:", nrow(dds), "\n")
cat("Genes removed         :", sum(!keep), "\n")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

In this section we do **not** perform statistical tests. The goal is **quality control:** check count distributions, detect technical outliers, and confirm that samples cluster as expected before committing to differential expression analysis.

### Estimate Size Factors

Library sizes (total mapped reads) differ between samples due to technical variation in sequencing depth. `DESeq2's` median-of-ratios normalisation corrects for this by computing a size factor per sample. Size factors close to 1.0 indicate balanced libraries; values far from 1.0 suggest uneven sequencing depth and warrant investigation.

```{r human-qc-size-factors-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)

sizeFactors(dds) %>%
  enframe(name = "sample", value = "size_factor") %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "DESeq2 size factors per sample") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

### Distribution of Normalised Counts

Boxplots of log2-normalised counts per sample provide a quick visual check that all samples have comparable expression distributions. After normalisation, boxes should overlap substantially. A sample that is a clear outlier in median or spread may indicate a failed library or mislabelled sample.

::: {style="background:#f8d7da;border-left:4px solid #721c24;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;"}
<strong>📌 Remember:</strong> These normalised counts are for visualisation only. Always feed DESeq2 <strong>raw integer counts</strong>.
:::

```{r human-qc-distribution-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
normalized_counts <- counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)

counts_norm <- reshape2::melt(
  normalized_counts,
  varnames   = c("gene_id", "sample"),
  value.name = "counts"
)

counts_norm <- inner_join(
  counts_norm,
  as.data.frame(colData(dds)),
  by = "sample"
)

dir.create(file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "plots"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

distribution <- ggplot(counts_norm,
                       aes(x    = sample,
                           y    = log2(counts + 1),
                           fill = condition)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_pubr(border = TRUE) +
  xlab("Sample") +
  ylab("log2(normalised counts + 1)") +
  ggtitle("Normalised count distribution - Human ASM")

distribution

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "plots", "normalised_count_distribution.png"),
  plot     = distribution,
  width    = 8,
  height   = 6,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

### Variance-Stabilising Transformation

The plots below compare samples to each other, and for that the counts need one more
step. In raw or normalised counts the highly expressed genes vary far more in absolute
terms than quiet ones, so they would dominate any distance or PCA calculation. The
variance-stabilising transformation (VST) removes that dependence between a gene's mean
and its variance, so every gene contributes on a comparable scale
([Anders & Huber, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2010-11-10-r106)).

```{r human-qc-vst-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
vsd <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds, blind = TRUE)
```

:::boxy
**`blind = TRUE`** computes the transformation ignoring the experimental design. That is
what you want for QC: an unbiased view of how samples relate, not one shaped by the answer
you are hoping for. Use `blind = FALSE` only when the transformed values feed a model that
already accounts for the design.
:::

### Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA reduces the high-dimensional expression space (one dimension per gene) to a small number of principal components that capture the largest sources of variance in the data. Inspect whether the treatment separates samples, and whether donor identity contributes to the remaining structure.

If a nuisance variable (batch, sequencing run, RNA quality, or here the donor) carries a large share of the variance, it should be accounted for in the design before differential expression analysis ([Leek *et al.*, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrg2825)). Look at where it lands rather than assuming: a nuisance variable on PC1 is a warning, on a later component it is simply something the model should absorb.

```{r human-qc-pca-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
pca_data <- plotPCA(vsd,
                    intgroup  = c("sample", "condition", "donor"),
                    returnData = TRUE)

pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_data, "percentVar"), 1)

PCAPlot <- ggplot(pca_data, aes(x     = PC1,
                                y     = PC2,
                                color = condition,
                                shape = donor,
                                label = sample)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.8, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.3) +
  theme_pubr(border = TRUE) +
  theme(
    axis.text       = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title      = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  labs(
    x     = paste0("PC1: ", pct_var[1], "% variance"),
    y     = paste0("PC2: ", pct_var[2], "% variance"),
    title = "PCA - Human ASM (VST-transformed counts)",
    color = "Condition",
    shape = "Donor"
  )

PCAPlot

ggsave(
  filename = file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "plots", "PCA_Plot.png"),
  plot     = PCAPlot,
  width    = 8,
  height   = 6,
  dpi      = 300
)
```

:::boxy
**How to read this plot.** Each point is one sample; points close together have similar overall
expression. Check the **% variance** printed on each axis first - it tells you how much of the total
variation that axis carries, so a separation on PC1 means more than the same-looking separation on PC3.
Here colour encodes treatment and shape encodes donor. If treatment separates cleanly on one axis while
donors are spread along another, that is the classic signature of a paired design: a consistent treatment
effect on top of donor-to-donor baseline differences.
:::

### Top Variable Genes Heatmap

Clustering the 50 most variable genes across samples provides a gene-level view of the structure in the data. Truly treatment-responsive genes should show block structure by condition. This heatmap also helps reveal whether donor identity contributes strongly to the top variable genes.

Row-scaling (z-score per gene) is applied so that highly expressed genes do not visually dominate over lowly expressed ones.

```{r human-qc-topvar-heatmap-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=12}

topVarGenes <- head(order(rowVars(assay(vsd)), decreasing = TRUE), 50)

df_anno <- as.data.frame(colData(vsd)[, c("condition", "donor"), drop = FALSE])

# The metadata does not record donor sex, but the data do: Y-chromosome genes are
# expressed only in cells from male donors.
y_genes <- intersect(c("RPS4Y1", "DDX3Y", "KDM5D", "USP9Y"), rownames(vsd))
y_expr  <- colMeans(assay(vsd)[y_genes, , drop = FALSE])
df_anno$sex_inferred <- ifelse(y_expr > mean(range(y_expr)), "male", "female")

heat_plot <- pheatmap(
  assay(vsd)[topVarGenes, ],
  cluster_cols             = TRUE,
  cluster_rows             = TRUE,
  scale                    = "row",
  clustering_distance_rows = "euclidean",
  clustering_distance_cols = "euclidean",
  annotation_col           = df_anno,
  show_colnames            = TRUE,
  show_rownames            = TRUE,
  fontsize_row             = 7,
  main                     = "Top 50 variable genes - Human ASM (VST, row-scaled)"
)

heat_plot

png(
  filename = file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "plots", "heatmap_top50_variable.png"),
  width    = 8,
  height   = 12,
  units    = "in",
  res      = 300
)
heat_plot
dev.off()
```

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> Rows are gene symbols (from the human reference), so they can be used
  directly in the enrichment analysis (script 03) with no ID conversion step. A small number of
  genes have no agreed symbol yet, and GENCODE gives those its ENSEMBL identifier as the name
  instead; those rows simply will not match anything in the gene set databases.
</div>

<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ Three things in this plot are not biology - spot them before you interpret it.</strong>
  <ul>
    <li><strong>Names ending in <code>.1</code>, <code>.2</code>, ...</strong> (e.g. <code>TXLNGY.1</code>):
    a few symbols belong to more than one gene ID in the annotation, so R made the row names unique by
    appending a number.</li>
    <li><strong>Rows named <code>ENSG...</code></strong>: these genes have no agreed symbol yet, so the
    annotation uses their ENSEMBL identifier as the name. They are real genes, just unnamed ones.</li>
    <li><strong>Sex-linked genes</strong> (e.g. <code>RPS4Y1</code>, <code>DDX3Y</code>,
    <code>KDM5D</code>, <code>USP9Y</code>): the four donors are not all the same sex (the <code>sex_inferred</code> bar is derived from these genes), so these genes are
    among the most "variable" in the whole dataset - a donor property, unrelated to dexamethasone.</li>
  </ul>
  Most-variable is <em>not</em> most-relevant: the drug-response rows (look for <code>FKBP5</code>,
  <code>ZBTB16</code>, <code>GPX3</code>) sit next to rows that only separate donors. That is why the next notebook tests a
  specific contrast instead of trusting variance.
</div>

:::boxy
**How to read this heatmap:**

- Each **row** is a gene, each **column** is a sample
- Colours show the **z-score** (row-scaled expression) - red = higher than average for that gene, blue = lower
- The **dendrograms** show hierarchical clustering - samples/genes that behave similarly are grouped together

**What to look for:**

- Clear colour blocks by condition → the treatment has a strong, consistent transcriptional effect
- Whether samples cluster by donor instead of (or in addition to) treatment - a visual argument for the paired design
:::

## Summary

Before proceeding to differential expression analysis, confirm the QC checks and note the design implication:

:::boxy
| Check | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| Size factors ≈ 1.0 across samples | Library sizes are balanced |
| Boxplots of normalised counts overlap | No extreme outlier samples |
| Correlation heatmap | Note whether structure is by treatment, by donor, or both |
| PCA | Note whether treatment or donor drives the main axes |
| No isolated samples | No technical outliers |
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em; color: grey;"}
*Because the four donors each contribute a treated and an untreated sample, donor is a paired factor.
The recommended design `~ donor + condition` removes donor baseline differences before testing the
treatment effect. Script 02 runs this model and, for teaching, compares it against the simpler
`~ condition` model.*
:::


<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ Important:</strong> If any check fails, investigate the cause before running DESeq2. Proceeding with outlier samples or a mis-specified design will compromise all downstream results.
</div>


```{r human-qc-export-dds-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ── Export DDS for downstream analysis ────────────────────────────────────────
results_dir <- file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "rds")
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

dds_path <- file.path(results_dir, "dds_human_asm.rds")
saveRDS(dds, file = dds_path)
```


```{r, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
cat("✅ DDS saved to:", dds_path, "\n")
cat("   Dimensions  :", nrow(dds), "genes ×", ncol(dds), "samples\n")
cat("   Design      : ~ donor + condition\n")
cat("   Conditions  :", paste(levels(dds$condition), collapse = " vs "), "\n")
```

## Interpretation questions

::: question
1. Find each donor's treated and untreated points in your PCA. Which is bigger: the difference between donors, or the shift caused by treatment? Based on that, predict which model will find more differentially expressed genes in the next notebook - `~ condition` or `~ donor + condition` - and why. Write the prediction down: you will check it.
2. Pick the gene with the cleanest treated/untreated split in your heatmap. Which of these can you claim from it: more transcript? more protein? more activity? Then look for *NR3C1* - the receptor dexamethasone binds to. It is a pre-existing protein: did its transcript need to change for the response you see? What does that say about what RNA-seq can and cannot show?
:::

# Differential Expression Analysis

This report covers differential expression (DE) analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from primary human airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells treated with dexamethasone ([Himes *et al.*, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0099625)) using `DESeq2`.

We test one contrast:

::: boxy
- **Dexamethasone (treatment) vs untreated (control)** - which genes change expression in response to the glucocorticoid?
:::

::: {style="background:#eaf4fd;border-left:5px solid #3498db;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;border-radius:6px;"}
<strong>⭐ Important:</strong> This script assumes you have already run `01_quality_control.Rmd` and that the `dds` object has been saved. If not, re-run the QC script first.
:::

::: {style="background:#fff3cd;border-left:4px solid #ffc107;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;"}
<strong>🎓 Teaching design.</strong> Each donor contributes a treated and an untreated sample, so donor
is a paired factor. We run two models:
<ul>
<li><strong>Paired (recommended):</strong> <code>~ donor + condition</code> - adjusts for donor baseline before testing treatment.</li>
<li><strong>Simple (for comparison):</strong> <code>~ condition</code> - ignores donor.</li>
</ul>
Comparing them shows how accounting for a known confounder changes power and the gene list.
The paired model is used for all downstream analysis.
:::

**Setup the Environment**

```{r human-de-libraries, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(DESeq2)
library(ggpubr)
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(DT)
```


## Running DESeq2

<div style="background:#f8d7da;border-left:4px solid #721c24;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;">
  <strong>⚠️ Warning:</strong> Always use raw integer counts as input. Do not use TPM, FPKM, or any normalised values - DESeq2 handles normalisation internally.
</div>

`DESeq2` fits a negative binomial model to the raw counts and performs a Wald test for each gene. Internally it runs three steps in sequence: size factor estimation (normalisation), dispersion estimation, and the Wald test. These can also be run separately, but `DESeq()` handles all three in one call.

<details>
<summary><strong>What DESeq2 does internally - three steps</strong> (click to expand)</summary>

**1. Size factor estimation (normalisation)**

Each sample gets a size factor that accounts for differences in sequencing depth.
DESeq2 uses the **median-of-ratios** method: for each gene, it computes the ratio
of each sample's count to the geometric mean count across all samples, then takes
the median ratio across all genes as the size factor. This is more robust than
simply dividing by total counts because it is not affected by a small number of
highly expressed genes dominating the library.

**2. Dispersion estimation**

RNA-seq count data is overdispersed - the variance is greater than the mean
(unlike a Poisson distribution which assumes variance = mean). DESeq2 models
this with a **negative binomial distribution** and estimates a dispersion
parameter per gene, which describes how much counts vary between replicates
beyond what is expected by chance. Genes with few replicates get their
dispersion estimates shrunk toward a fitted trend across all genes
(**empirical Bayes shrinkage**) - this stabilises estimates for genes with
low counts.

**3. Wald test**

For each gene, DESeq2 fits the negative binomial model and tests whether the
log2 fold change between conditions is significantly different from zero using
a **Wald test**. The resulting p-values are then corrected for multiple testing
using the **Benjamini-Hochberg** procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR).

---

**Why does the order matter?**

With the design `~ donor + condition`, the last term is the one tested. `resultsNames(dds)`
will list `condition_treatment_vs_control` - the fold change is calculated as **treatment / control**:

- **Positive LFC** → gene is upregulated in dexamethasone-treated cells
- **Negative LFC** → gene is downregulated in dexamethasone-treated cells

If control were not set as the reference level, the fold change would be
inverted and your biological interpretation would be backwards.

</details>

```{r human-de-load-dds, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
git_root <- system("git rev-parse --show-toplevel", intern = TRUE)

dds <- readRDS(file.path(git_root, "results", "human", "rds", "dds_human_asm.rds"))

cat("✅ DDS loaded\n")
cat("   Dimensions  :", nrow(dds), "genes ×", ncol(dds), "samples\n")
cat("   Design      :", paste(deparse(design(dds)), collapse = ""), "\n")
cat("   Conditions  :", paste(levels(dds$condition), collapse = " vs "), "\n")
```

<div style="background:#d1ecf1;border-left:4px solid #0c5460;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> The variable of interest is at the end of the design formula, and the control group is the first (reference) factor level. Both were set in the QC script.
</div>

### Factor Order and Reference Level

Before fitting, make sure the comparison points the way you think it does.
The first factor level is always the reference (denominator) in `DESeq2` comparisons. Setting it explicitly ensures fold changes are computed in the intended direction: **treatment (dexamethasone) vs control (untreated)**, not the reverse.

```{r human-de-factor-order-0, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

dds$condition <- relevel(dds$condition, ref = "control")

levels(dds$condition)
```

::: {style="background:#d4edda;border-left:4px solid #28a745;padding:10px;margin:10px 0;"}
<strong>📌 Remember:</strong> The reference level determines the direction of fold changes. A positive log2FC means higher expression in dexamethasone-treated cells relative to untreated.
:::


**Run DESeq2 (paired design)**
```{r human-de-run-deseq, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)
```

**Did the model behave?**

`DESeq()` estimates how variable each gene is between replicates (its dispersion), then
pulls the noisy per-gene estimates towards the overall trend. This plot is where you check
that it worked.

```{r human-de-disp-plot, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
plotDispEsts(dds, main = "Dispersion estimates")
```

:::boxy
**How to read it.** Each black dot is one gene, placed by its mean expression (left to right)
and its dispersion (bottom to top). The red line is the trend DESeq2 fitted across all genes.
The blue dots are the final estimates, pulled from the black dots towards that line - the pull
is strongest for low-count genes on the left, where a single odd replicate can otherwise make
a gene look far more variable than it really is. Points circled in blue were left alone,
treated as genuinely variable rather than noisy.

What you want to see: dispersion falling as expression rises, and blue dots hugging the red
line. A cloud with no trend means the model has not fitted well, and nothing downstream is
trustworthy.
:::

## Teaching Comparison: Paired vs Simple Design

Before extracting the final results, we fit the simple `~ condition` model on the same data and compare how many genes each design calls significant. This makes the effect of accounting for donor concrete.

```{r human-de-design-comparison, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Simple model: drop the donor term
dds_simple <- dds
design(dds_simple) <- ~ condition
dds_simple <- DESeq(dds_simple)

res_paired_tmp <- results(dds,
                          contrast = c("condition", "treatment", "control"),
                          alpha    = 0.05)
res_simple_tmp <- results(dds_simple,
                          contrast = c("condition", "treatment", "control"),
                          alpha    = 0.05)

n_sig <- function(r) sum(r$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

comparison_tbl <- data.frame(
  Design            = c("~ donor + condition (paired)", "~ condition (simple)"),
  `Significant genes (padj < 0.05)` = c(n_sig(res_paired_tmp), n_sig(res_simple_tmp)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(comparison_tbl, caption = "Effect of design on the number of significant genes") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

:::boxy
**How to read this comparison.** Pairing on donor removes the between-donor baseline variation from
the residual, which usually *lowers* the per-gene noise and *increases* power to detect the treatment
effect. If the paired model calls more genes significant here, that is the mechanism. If the two are
similar, donor happened to explain little variance in this subset - but the paired model is still the
correct specification given the experimental design, so we keep it.
:::

::: {style="background:#eaf4fd;border-left:5px solid #3498db;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;border-radius:6px;"}
**What we see in this dataset.** The paired model (`~ donor + condition`) calls roughly **4,150**
genes significant at padj < 0.05, versus about **2,900** for the simple model (`~ condition`) - an
increase of around 1,300 genes (~45%). This is a large, concrete demonstration of the paired-design
benefit: the four donors differ substantially in their baseline expression, and once that donor
variation is accounted for, the treatment signal becomes much easier to detect. This is exactly the
inter-patient variability the study design anticipated, and it is why we use the paired model for all
downstream steps.
:::

## Extracting Results

`results()` extracts the Wald test output for a given contrast. By default DESeq2 applies **independent filtering** - it removes genes with very low mean counts before multiple testing correction, which increases power to detect DE genes at a given FDR threshold.

We set `alpha = 0.05` to optimise filtering for a 5% FDR cutoff.

```{r human-de-extract-results, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
res <- results(dds,
               contrast = c("condition", "treatment", "control"),
               alpha    = 0.05)

summary(res)
```

We report genes that change by at least 2-fold, so that is what we should test for. The call above
asks whether the fold change differs from **zero**; a gene can clear that bar comfortably and still
be nowhere near 2-fold. Filtering the output afterwards on `|log2FC| >= 1` does not fix this,
because the filter is applied to the estimate, not to the hypothesis: nothing bounds how many genes
with a true change below 2-fold slip through on a lucky estimate.

`results()` can test against the threshold directly. `lfcThreshold = 1` moves the null hypothesis
from "no change" to "no more than 2-fold", and `altHypothesis = "greaterAbs"` asks for changes
larger than that in either direction. The adjusted p-values then control the error rate for the
claim we actually make.

```{r human-de-extract-results-threshold, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
res_thr <- results(dds,
                   contrast      = c("condition", "treatment", "control"),
                   lfcThreshold  = 1,
                   altHypothesis = "greaterAbs",
                   alpha         = 0.05)

summary(res_thr)
```

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> We keep both results objects. <code>res_thr</code> decides significance.
  <code>res</code> still provides the Wald statistic used to rank genes for GSEA in script 03 - that
  ranking must stay on the test against zero, because with a threshold the statistic is pulled to
  zero for every gene near the boundary and the ranking would be distorted.
</div>

::: {style="background:#eaf4fd;border-left:5px solid #3498db;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;border-radius:6px;"}
**Reading the summary.** Of 16,238 tested genes, about **2,290 are up** and **1,870 are down** at
padj < 0.05 (roughly 14% and 11%). Two lines are worth noting: **outliers = 0** means no gene was
flagged by Cook's distance as driven by a single extreme sample, and **low counts = 0** means
independent filtering did not need to remove additional low-expression genes (the pre-filtering in
script 01 already handled them). A large but balanced set of up- and down-regulated genes is the
expected signature of a strong, genome-wide treatment response - dexamethasone is a potent
transcriptional regulator, so this magnitude is biologically plausible.
:::

The results table contains one row per gene with the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `baseMean` | Mean normalised count across all samples |
| `log2FoldChange` | log2(treatment / control) |
| `lfcSE` | Standard error of the log2FC estimate |
| `stat` | Wald statistic |
| `pvalue` | Raw p-value |
| `padj` | Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value |

---

### Log2 Fold Change Shrinkage

:::boxy
**What is this step and why do we need it?**

 After running DESeq2, every gene gets a raw log2 fold change (LFC) estimate.
 For **lowly expressed genes**, these estimates are unreliable - a gene with
 1 count in control and 3 in treatment looks like a 3-fold change, but this
 is just noise from low counts.

 `lfcShrink()` corrects this using **empirical Bayes shrinkage**: it pulls
 noisy estimates (low counts, high uncertainty) toward zero, while leaving
 well-supported fold changes (high counts, consistent signal) largely
 unchanged. Think of it as a confidence-weighted adjustment.
<div class="important">
  <strong>⭐ Important:</strong> shrinkage changes the fold-change estimates, nothing else. It never
 computes a p-value of its own.

 Keeping track of which number comes from where is worth a moment, because we now have three objects:
 `res` tests against zero and supplies the Wald statistic that script 03 ranks genes by; `res_thr`
 tests against the 2-fold threshold and supplies the p-values that decide significance; `res_shrunk`
 supplies the fold changes. The table built below takes each from its own source.

 So shrinkage no longer decides which genes qualify. It decides what the fold changes look like, which
 is what the volcano, the MA plot and the heatmap show you.
</div>

 **Why `apeglm`?** Three shrinkage methods exist in DESeq2:
 - `apeglm` - most accurate for simple two-group comparisons like ours ✅
 - `ashr` - more flexible; needed when comparing two non-reference groups
 - `normal` - the original method, now outdated and not recommended

 For a treatment vs control design, `apeglm` is the right choice.
 See [Zhu *et al.*, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btz585) for benchmarks.
:::
```{r human-de-lfc-shrink, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Pass res = res so the shrunken object inherits the p-values and independent
# filtering from the results() call above (alpha = 0.05) instead of recomputing
# them at apeglm's default alpha.
res_shrunk <- lfcShrink(dds,
                        coef  = "condition_treatment_vs_control",
                        type  = "apeglm",
                        res   = res)

summary(res_shrunk, alpha = 0.05)
```

---

### Sorting and Filtering Significant Genes

We order genes by adjusted p-value and keep those with **padj < 0.05** from the thresholded test.
There is no separate fold-change filter: the 2-fold requirement is already part of the hypothesis.

```{r human-de-filter-results, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
res_df <- as.data.frame(res_shrunk) %>%
  rownames_to_column("gene") %>%
  mutate(
    stat   = res[gene, "stat"],         # Wald statistic vs zero; lfcShrink() drops it. Ranks genes for GSEA in script 03
    pvalue = res_thr[gene, "pvalue"],   # significance comes from the test against the 2-fold threshold
    padj   = res_thr[gene, "padj"]
  ) %>%
  arrange(padj) %>%
  filter(!is.na(padj))

# No fold-change filter here: the 2-fold requirement is already inside the test.
res_sig <- res_df %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05)

cat("Total genes tested        :", nrow(res_df), "\n")
cat("Significant genes         :", nrow(res_sig), "\n")
cat("  Upregulated             :", sum(res_sig$log2FoldChange > 0), "\n")
cat("  Downregulated           :", sum(res_sig$log2FoldChange < 0), "\n")
```

::: {style="background:#eaf4fd;border-left:5px solid #3498db;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;border-radius:6px;"}
**What testing against the threshold does.** Testing against zero called ~4,150 genes at
padj < 0.05. Requiring the change to be *significantly* larger than 2-fold leaves **238** genes
(145 up, 93 down).

It is worth seeing how much of a difference the hypothesis makes. Filtering the old way - padj from
the test against zero, then `|log2FC| >= 1` on the shrunken estimates - gave **784** genes. Of those,
547 do not survive the proper test. They are not errors: their fold changes really do look larger than
2-fold. There is simply not enough evidence to say they *exceed* 2-fold rather than sitting just above
it by chance. Only one gene is gained.

So the shorter list is not a stricter cutoff applied to the same question. It is the answer to the
question we were claiming to ask all along.
:::

**Biological sanity check - known dexamethasone-responsive genes**

Himes *et al.* highlighted several well-established glucocorticoid-responsive genes. We check where they
land in our results rather than assuming - if the pipeline is working, these should be significant and in
the expected direction (dexamethasone typically *induces* these).

```{r human-de-known-genes-check, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
known_genes <- c("DUSP1", "KLF15", "PER1", "TSC22D3", "CRISPLD2", "FKBP5", "ZBTB16")

res_df %>%
  filter(gene %in% known_genes) %>%
  select(gene, log2FoldChange, padj) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))) %>%
  arrange(padj) %>%
  kable(caption = "Known glucocorticoid-responsive genes in our results") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
```

::: {style="background:#d4edda;border-left:4px solid #28a745;padding:0.5em 1em;margin:1em 0;border-radius:6px;"}
**How to read this.** If these canonical genes appear with positive log2FC and small padj, it is strong
evidence the analysis is capturing real glucocorticoid biology, not noise. A gene missing from the table
was filtered out earlier for low counts (not expressed in these cells); that is not a problem in itself.
In this dataset all of the recovered markers are strongly **induced** (positive log2FC) and highly
significant - including FKBP5, TSC22D3 (GILZ) and ZBTB16, three of the most reliable glucocorticoid-response
genes, and CRISPLD2, the gene the original study is named after. This is the expected positive-control
result and confirms the pipeline is working correctly.
:::

<div class="note">
  <strong>📘 Note:</strong> Known dexamethasone-responsive genes reported by Himes <em>et al.</em>
  include <em>DUSP1</em>, <em>KLF15</em>, <em>PER1</em>, <em>TSC22D3</em> and <em>CRISPLD2</em>.
  Checking whether these appear among your top hits is a good biological sanity check - but let the analysis produce them rather than assuming their rank.
</div>

---

**Interactive Results Table**

```{r human-de-results-table, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
DT::datatable(
  # signif(), not round(): round(padj, 4) prints every p-value below 0.00005
  # as a flat 0, which looks like the test returned zero. It never does.
  res_sig %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))),
  rownames   = FALSE,
  extensions = c('Buttons', 'Scroller'),
  options    = list(
    dom         = 'Bfrtip',
    buttons     = c('copy', 'csv'),
    scrollX     = TRUE,
    scrollY     = 300,
    scroller    = TRUE
  ),
  caption = 'Significant DE genes - dexamethasone vs untreated (padj < 0.05, |LFC| ≥ 1)'
)
```

## Visualisation

**Volcano Plot**

A volcano plot combines fold change (x-axis) and statistical significance (y-axis) into a single view. Genes in the upper corners are both strongly and significantly changed - these are the most biologically interesting candidates.

The dashed lines mark |log2FC| = 1 and padj = 0.05. Note that points are now coloured by padj alone,
because the 2-fold requirement is inside the test: a gene to the right of the line is not significant
unless it also clears padj, and the vertical line is a reference, no longer part of the rule.

```{r human-de-volcano, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
res_df <- res_df %>%
  mutate(
    significance = case_when(
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "Up",
      padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < 0 ~ "Down",
      TRUE                             ~ "NS"
    )
  )

top_labels <- res_df %>%
  filter(significance != "NS") %>%
  slice_min(padj, n = 10)

volcano <- ggplot(res_df, aes(x = log2FoldChange,
                              y = -log10(padj),
                              color = significance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1),  linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  geom_text(data = top_labels,
            aes(label = gene),
            size = 2.8, vjust = -0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Up" = "red", "Down" = "blue", "NS" = "grey70")) +
  theme_pubr(border = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano Plot - Dexamethasone vs Untreated",
    x     = "log2(Fold Change)",
    y     = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
    color = NULL
  )

volcano
```



### MA Plot

An MA plot shows log2 fold change (y-axis) against mean expression (x-axis). It helps assess whether the fold change estimates are stable across the expression range. After shrinkage, estimates for lowly expressed genes (left side) should be pulled toward zero.

The coloured points are the significant genes. `lfcShrink()` copies the p-values across untouched, so the shrunken object still carries the ones from the test against zero. We swap in the p-values from the test against the 2-fold threshold, so the plot marks the same genes the rest of the chapter calls significant rather than several thousand more.

```{r human-de-ma-plot, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
res_ma       <- res_shrunk
res_ma$padj  <- res_thr[rownames(res_ma), "padj"]   # colour by the thresholded test

# The default y-axis stops near +/-2.4 and draws everything beyond it as a
# triangle on the border - 109 genes here, including the strongest hits, which
# reach -8.9 and +10.9. +/-8 leaves only 3 genes off-scale.
plotMA(res_ma,
       alpha = 0.05,
       ylim  = c(-8, 8),
       main  = "MA Plot - Dexamethasone vs Untreated (shrunken LFC)",
       ylab  = "log2 Fold Change")
abline(h = c(-1, 1), lty = 2, col = "black")
```

### Top Gene Count Plot

Plotting raw normalised counts for the most significant gene provides a sanity check: the direction and magnitude of the fold change should be visually obvious. If it isn't, investigate further.

```{r human-de-top-gene, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
top_gene <- res_sig$gene[1]

plotCounts(dds,
           gene     = top_gene,
           intgroup = "condition",
           main     = paste("Normalised counts -", top_gene))
```


### Heatmap of Significant Genes

Clustering significant DE genes across samples provides a gene-level view of the expression differences. Genes should show clear block structure: high expression in treatment and low in control (or vice versa). With the paired design, you can also annotate donor to see whether the treatment effect is consistent across donors.

```{r human-de-de-heatmap, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=12}
vsd <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds, blind = FALSE)

sig_genes <- res_sig %>%
  slice_min(padj, n = min(50, nrow(res_sig))) %>%
  pull(gene)

df_anno    <- as.data.frame(colData(vsd)[, c("condition", "donor"), drop = FALSE])

pheatmap(
  assay(vsd)[sig_genes, ],
  cluster_cols             = TRUE,
  cluster_rows             = TRUE,
  scale                    = "row",
  clustering_distance_rows = "euclidean",
  clustering_distance_cols = "euclidean",
  annotation_col           = df_anno,
  show_colnames            = TRUE,
  show_rownames            = TRUE,
  fontsize_row             = 7,
  main                     = "Top DE genes - Dexamethasone vs Untreated (VST, row-scaled)"
)
```

## Saving Results

```{r human-de-save-results, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
results_dir <- file.path(git_root, "results", "human")
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

write.table(
  res_df,
  file      = file.path(results_dir, "DE_treatment_vs_control_all.tsv"),
  sep       = "\t",
  quote     = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

write.table(
  res_sig,
  file      = file.path(results_dir, "DE_treatment_vs_control_significant.tsv"),
  sep       = "\t",
  quote     = FALSE,
  row.names = FALSE
)

cat("Results saved to:", results_dir, "\n")
```

---

## Summary

| Step | Decision made |
|---|---|
| Design formula | `~ donor + condition` (paired); `~ condition` shown for comparison |
| Contrast | dexamethasone (treatment) vs untreated (control) |
| LFC shrinkage | `apeglm` method |
| Significance threshold | padj < 0.05 |
| Fold change threshold | tested, not filtered: `lfcThreshold = 1`, `altHypothesis = "greaterAbs"` |
| Enrichment (next script) | GSEA with `fgsea` and MSigDB Reactome sets |

Significant genes are saved and ready for gene set enrichment analysis in the next script.

## Interpretation questions

::: question
1. Your table shows the paired model (`~ donor + condition`) finds over a thousand more significant genes than the simple model - same data, same treatment. What changed? Where did the donor-to-donor differences "go" in the simple model, and why does giving them a name in the paired model make the treatment effect easier to see? Was your prediction from the QC notebook right?
2. Dexamethasone works by binding the glucocorticoid receptor, made by the gene *NR3C1*. Before looking: predict where *NR3C1* sits in your results - top hit, modest, or absent? Now find it in `res_df` (not the interactive table - that only holds genes passing *both* cutoffs). Two surprises are waiting: which **direction** did it move, and does it appear in your significant table at all? The drug did not switch this gene on - it bound the protein that was already there. So what did your RNA-seq actually measure about the receptor, and what did it miss?
:::
